Data type support and mappings vary depending on the connector. Refer to the connector documentation for more information.
This type captures boolean values true and false.
Integer numbers can be expressed as numeric literals in the following formats:
Hexadecimal integer composed of 0X or 0x and the value. Examples are 0x0A for decimal 10 or 0x11 for decimal 17.
Octal integer composed of 0O or 0o and the value. Examples are 0o40 for decimal 32 or 0o11 for decimal 9.
Binary integer composed of 0B or 0b and the value. Examples are 0b1001 for decimal 9 or 0b101010 for decimal `42``.

Underscore characters are ignored within literal values, and can be used to increase readability. For example, decimal integer 123_456 is equivalent to 123456. Preceding underscores, trailing under...
Integers are supported by the following data types.
A 8-bit signed two’s complement integer with a minimum value of -2^7 or -0x80 and a maximum value of 2^7 - 1 or 0x7F.
A 16-bit signed two’s complement integer with a minimum value of -2^15 or -0x8000 and a maximum value of 2^15 - 1 or 0x7FFF.
A 32-bit signed two’s complement integer with a minimum value of -2^31 or -0x80000000 and a maximum value of 2^31 - 1 or 0x7FFFFFFF. The names INTEGER and INT can both be used for this type.
A 64-bit signed two’s complement integer with a minimum value of -2^63 or -0x8000000000000000 and a maximum value of 2^63 - 1 or 0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF.

A real is a 32-bit inexact, variable-precision implementing the IEEE Standard 754 for Binary Floating-Point Arithmetic.
A double is a 64-bit inexact, variable-precision implementing the IEEE Standard 754 for Binary Floating-Point Arithmetic.
A floating point, decimal number of unspecified precision of at least 50 decimal digits. The type supports positive values as small as 1e-100 or smaller, and values as large as 1e100 or larger.
The NUMBER type supports the special values Infinity, -Infinity, and NaN, following similar semantics to floating-point types:
SELECT NUMBER 'Infinity'; -- Infinity SELECT NUMBER '-Infinity'; -- -Infinity SELECT NUMBER 'NaN'; -- NaN
Division by zero raises a “Division by zero” error:
SELECT NUMBER '1' / NUMBER '0'; -- ERROR: Division by zero
NaN is not equal to any value, including itself:
Ordering follows the convention: -Infinity < all finite values < Infinity < NaN.
Example literals: NUMBER '10.3', NUMBER '1234567890', NUMBER '1e3', NUMBER 'Infinity', NUMBER 'NaN'
Exact numeric values can be expressed as numeric literals such as 1.1, and are supported by the DECIMAL data type.

Leading zeros in literal values are permitted and ignored. For example, 000123.456 is equivalent to 123.456.
A exact decimal number. Precision up to 38 digits is supported but performance is best up to 18 digits.
The decimal type takes two literal parameters:
scale - number of digits in fractional part. Scale is optional and defaults to 0.
Variable length character data with an optional maximum length.
SQL statements support simple literal, as well as Unicode usage:
Unicode string with default escape character: U&'Hello winter \2603 !'
Unicode string with custom escape character: U&'Hello winter #2603 !' UESCAPE '#'

The following instance methods are available on VARCHAR values. Each returns a new value; the receiver is never modified. The related plain function is linked from each entry.
Returns the number of Unicode code points in string. Related: length(). SELECT 'Hello, World!'.length(); -- 13
Returns string with every character converted to lower case. Related: lower(). SELECT 'HELLO'.lower(); -- hello
Returns string with every character converted to upper case. Related: upper(). SELECT 'hello'.upper(); -- HELLO
Returns string with every occurrence of the substring search removed. Related: replace(). SELECT 'a.b.c'.replace('.'); -- abc
Returns string with every occurrence of the substring search replaced by replacement. Related: replace(). SELECT 'a.b.c'.replace('.', '-'); -- a-b-c
Returns string with its code points in reverse order. Related: reverse(). SELECT 'Trino'.reverse(); -- onirT
Splits string on each occurrence of delimiter and returns the pieces as an array. Related: split(). SELECT 'a,b,c'.split(','); -- [a, b, c]
Splits string on delimiter into at most limit pieces; the last piece holds the unsplit remainder. Related: split(). SELECT 'a,b,c'.split(',', 2); -- [a, b,c]
Returns true when string ends with suffix, otherwise false. Related: ends_with(). SELECT 'apple'.ends_with('ple'); -- true
Returns true when string begins with prefix, otherwise false. Related: starts_with(). SELECT 'apple'.starts_with('app'); -- true
Returns the 1-based index of the first occurrence of substring in string, or 0 when it does not occur. Related: strpos(). SELECT 'hello'.strpos('l'); -- 3
Returns the 1-based index of the instance-th occurrence of substring in string, or 0 when there are fewer than instance occurrences. Related: strpos(). SELECT 'hello'.strpos('l', 2); -- 4
Returns the part of string from the 1-based index start to the end. Related: substring(). SELECT 'Trino'.substring(2); -- rino
Returns the length code points of string beginning at the 1-based index start. Related: substring(). SELECT 'Trino'.substring(2, 2); -- ri

Returns string with each character that occurs in from replaced by the character at the same position in to, and removed when to is shorter. Related: translate(). SELECT 'abcd'.translate('ac', 'xy'...
Returns string with whitespace removed from both ends. Related: trim(). SELECT ' hi '.trim(); -- hi
Returns string with any of the characters in chars removed from both ends. Related: trim(). SELECT '##hi##'.trim('#'); -- hi
Returns string with whitespace removed from the start. Related: ltrim().
Returns string with any of the characters in chars removed from the start. Related: ltrim().
Returns string with whitespace removed from the end. Related: rtrim().
Returns string with any of the characters in chars removed from the end. Related: rtrim().
Returns string padded on the left with copies of padstring until it is size code points long, or truncated to size when already longer. Related: lpad(). SELECT '7'.lpad(3, '0'); -- 007
Returns string padded on the right with copies of padstring until it is size code points long, or truncated to size when already longer. Related: rpad(). SELECT '7'.rpad(3, '0'); -- 700
Returns the UTF-8 encoding of string as a VARBINARY value. Related: to_utf8().
The following static methods construct VARCHAR values:
Returns the one-character string whose only character has Unicode code point n. Related: chr(). SELECT varchar::chr(65); -- A

Returns the string decoded from the UTF-8 bytes in binary, with invalid byte sequences replaced by the Unicode replacement character. Related: from_utf8(). SELECT varchar::from_utf8(X'48656C6C6F');...
Returns the string decoded from the UTF-8 bytes in binary, with invalid byte sequences replaced by the string replace. Related: from_utf8().

JSON value type, which can be a JSON object, a JSON array, a JSON number, a JSON string, true, false or null.
A semi-structured value type. A VARIANT value can represent any of the following:
VARIANT is designed for working with semi-structured data efficiently, and is commonly used with connectors and file formats that support a native variant type.
VARIANT differs from JSON in that it preserves the full underlying value type, rather than reducing values to a limited set of JSON types.
SELECT typeof(CAST(JSON '{"a": 1, "b": [true, null]}' AS VARIANT)); -- variant SELECT CAST(CAST(JSON '123' AS VARIANT) AS BIGINT); -- 123
VARIANT follows the Apache Iceberg Variant specification. Trino implements this specification directly, including its type system, value encoding, and semantics.
This ensures consistent behavior when reading and writing variant values across systems that support the same specification.
See also VARIANT functions and operators

An array of the given component type.

A map between the given component types. A map is a collection of key-value pairs, where each key is associated with a single value. Map keys are required, while map values can be null.
More information in Map functions and operators.
A structure made up of fields that allows mixed types. The fields may be of any SQL type.
By default, row fields are not named, but names can be assigned.
Example: CAST(ROW(1, 2e0) AS ROW(x BIGINT, y DOUBLE))
Named row fields are accessed with field reference operator (.).
Example: CAST(ROW(1, 2.0) AS ROW(x BIGINT, y DOUBLE)).x
Named or unnamed row fields are accessed by position with the subscript operator ([]). The position starts at 1 and must be a constant.

Calculating the approximate distinct count can be done much more cheaply than an exact count using the HyperLogLog data sketch. See HyperLogLog functions.
A HyperLogLog sketch allows efficient computation of approx_distinct(). It starts as a sparse representation, switching to a dense representation when it becomes more efficient.
A P4HyperLogLog sketch is similar to HyperLogLog, but it starts (and remains) in the dense representation.
A SetDigest (setdigest) is a data sketch structure used in calculating Jaccard similarity coefficient between two sets.
MinHash with a single hash function
The HyperLogLog structure is used for the approximation of the distinct elements in the original set.
The MinHash structure is used to store a low memory footprint signature of the original set. The similarity of any two sets is estimated by comparing their signatures.
SetDigests are additive, meaning they can be merged together.
